content.text: Ultrasound is sound with frequencies too high for humans to hear, but it has remarkable applications in medicine, industry, and nature. From seeing babies before they're born to detecting flaws in metal structures, ultrasound technology harnesses the properties of high-frequency sound waves in ways that have transformed many fields.
is sound with frequencies above the upper limit of human hearing (above 20 kHz).
Same properties as audible sound (longitudinal wave, needs medium)
Very short wavelengths due to high frequency
Short wavelength allows detection of small features
Reflects off boundaries between different materials
Can penetrate materials that light cannot
A transducer produces a short pulse of ultrasound
The pulse travels into the body/material
At boundaries (where density changes), some ultrasound is reflected back
The transducer detects the returning echoes
Time delays and signal strengths are used to build an image

Ultrasound is preferred over X-rays for prenatal scans because it is non-ionising and does not damage living cells or DNA. X-rays are ionising and could harm a developing baby.

Comparing Ultrasound and X-rays for Medical Imaging
— Ultrasound is sound waves, not electromagnetic radiation. It's not ionising.
— Bats can see, but use echolocation in darkness for precision navigation.
— Higher frequency gives better resolution but less penetration. There's a trade-off.
— Ultrasound reflects strongly from bone, which is why it's not useful for imaging through bone.
— Ultrasound is used for many diagnostic purposes: heart, liver, muscles, blood vessels, etc.

Without gel, air between the transducer and skin would cause almost total reflection

of the ultrasound at the skin surface because of the large difference in density/acoustic impedance between air and skin. The gel removes the air gap and matches impedance, allowing the ultrasound to enter the body efficiently. (reasoning)
